cover.title: Docker Complete Handbook
cover.subtitle: From Basics to Advanced
cover.tagline: Package once, run the same on any host

items: Docker is ==client-server==: the `docker` CLI calls the `dockerd` daemon
They talk over a REST API on `/var/run/docker.sock`
A container is an isolated ==process== on the shared host kernel
A VM instead runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor
`dockerd` delegates container lifecycle to ==containerd==
`containerd` calls ==runc== to create the container process
runc is the **OCI** runtime: sets up namespaces and cgroups
Then runc execs your process and exits
==overlay2== is a union filesystem
It stacks read-only image layers
Plus one thin writable layer on top
Container writes land only in that top layer

lines: # runc execs: echo hi, then exit

items: Thinking a Linux container can run a **different kernel**
Thinking Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows is native
It runs a hidden ==Linux VM== underneath
Mounting `docker.sock` into a container: root-equivalent host control

blocks.title: Interview Point
blocks.text: How does Docker differ from a VM? What do namespaces and cgroups each do? What are containerd and runc?

items: Namespaces limit what a process **sees**
cgroups limit what a process **uses**
The shared ==host kernel== is why containers start fast
Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows hides a Linux VM

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: A container is a namespaced, cgroup-limited process on the shared kernel, started via CLI → dockerd → containerd → runc.

items: An ==image== is a read-only template: filesystem layers plus metadata
Metadata holds env, entrypoint and exposed ports
`RUN`, `COPY` and `ADD` each create a **layer**
Other instructions only add metadata, so they add no layer
Each layer is addressed by its ==SHA256 digest==
Identical layers are shared between images
So a shared layer is stored once and pulled once
The manifest lists the layers and the config
Multi-arch images use a manifest list (index)
A container gets one thin ==writable layer== on top
Editing a lower file **copies it up** first
The image layers below are never changed
Many containers share one image's layers

blocks.note: inspect prints JSON, not a table

items: Relying on `:latest`: it is **not** guaranteed newest, so builds drift
A later `rm` does not shrink the image: the earlier layer still holds the file
Fix: delete files in the same `RUN` that created them

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: What is a layer?
Tag vs digest: what is the difference?
Why does a later rm not reduce image size?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Images are stacked, digest-addressed, shared layers; pin digests and never trust :latest.

items: A ==container== is a running or stopped instance of an image
It owns a writable layer, a network and a process tree
`docker run` = create + start in one step
Common flags: `-d`, `-it`, `--rm`, `--name`, `-p`, `-e`, `-v`
==PID 1== is the main process; when it exits, the container stops
`docker stop` sends {blue:SIGTERM}, then SIGKILL after a 10s grace
`docker kill` sends **SIGKILL** immediately, with no cleanup
Limits: `--memory 512m`, `--cpus 1.5`, `--pids-limit`
Going over the memory limit gets the process **OOM-killed**
Restart policies: `no`, `on-failure[:N]`, `always`, `unless-stopped`

blocks.text: 5. run vs start, exec vs attach

items: Shell-form CMD runs under `sh`, which drops SIGTERM, so stops take 10s; use ==exec form==
Expecting data to survive `docker rm`; the writable layer dies with the container
Starting a background daemon: PID 1 exits and the container stops

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: What happens on docker stop?
Difference between exec and attach?
Why does a container exit immediately?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: A container lives and dies with PID 1: stop it with SIGTERM, cap it with limits, and keep data in volumes.

items: A ==Dockerfile== is a text recipe of instructions
`docker build` turns that recipe into an image
`FROM` sets the base image
`WORKDIR` sets the working directory
`COPY` adds files from the build context
`RUN` executes at build time and creates a layer
`CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` define the runtime command
`ENV` is set at runtime; `ARG` is __build-time only__
`EXPOSE` documents a port; it does **not** publish it
`USER` switches to non-root for later steps and runtime

blocks.text: 4. COPY vs ADD, Shell vs Exec

items: Prefer ==COPY==: it only copies files from the context
`ADD` also extracts local tars and fetches URLs: surprising
Shell form `RUN npm start` runs through `/bin/sh -c`
Exec form `["npm","start"]` has **no shell** and handles signals correctly
No `.dockerignore`: `node_modules` and `.git` enter the build context
Secrets in `ENV` or `ARG` stay visible in `docker history`
Assuming `EXPOSE 3000` publishes it; you still need `-p`
Shell-form `CMD` leaves `sh` as PID 1, so SIGTERM is lost

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: which is overridable, and how do they combine?
ARG vs ENV: which survives into the running container?
Does EXPOSE publish a port?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Write exec-form instructions, prefer COPY, keep secrets out of the image, and ignore junk with .dockerignore.

items: `ENV` persists at runtime; `ARG` vanishes after build
Use `.dockerignore` to skip `node_modules` and `.git`
A layer is ==reused== if its instruction and input files are unchanged
One cache **miss** invalidates every layer after it
Order instructions least to most frequently changing: base, manifests, install, source
Copy `package.json` or `requirements.txt` first, then install
Copy source last, so code edits skip the ==reinstall==
Edit code only: top layers hit cache, one layer rebuilds
Build in a fat stage with compilers and SDKs
`COPY --from=builder` moves only the artifacts to a slim runtime stage
The final image ships the binary, not the build tools
Go example: ~800MB golang image becomes ~**10MB** on scratch

blocks.note: scratch has no shell or libc

items: Combine related commands in one `RUN` with `&&`
Clean in that layer: `apt-get clean`, `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`
==.dockerignore== shrinks the context and avoids needless invalidation
BuildKit runs stages in parallel and skips unused stages
`--mount=type=cache` keeps pip downloads; `--mount=type=secret` keeps tokens out of layers

blocks.title: 6. Common Mistakes
items: `COPY . .` before install busts the cache on every code change
`apt-get update` in its own `RUN` leaves a stale cached index
Fix: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y` in one `RUN`

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: How do you shrink an image?
Why does instruction order matter?
What does multi-stage solve?
`docker build --no-cache .` forces a full rebuild
`docker build --target builder .` stops at one stage
`docker image ls` compares the sizes of your tags

blocks.title: Size Check
blocks.text: Run `docker history <image>` to spot the fattest layer.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Stable layers first, build in a fat stage, ship only the artifacts.

items: The container's ==writable layer== dies with the container
Writes go through copy-on-write, so they are **slower**
Persistent data needs a ==volume== or a mount
`docker rm` on a container wipes its layer
==Named volume==: Docker-managed under `/var/lib/docker/volumes`
==Bind mount==: maps a host path in, ideal for dev live-reload
==tmpfs==: host memory only, gone on stop, good for secrets
Volume **drivers** (NFS, cloud block storage) give shared or remote storage
An empty ==named volume== is seeded from the image path
A **bind mount** hides the image's files at that path

blocks.note: throwaway container tars volume to host

items: **Bind mount in production**: UID/permission and path-portability breaks
`docker compose down -v` ==silently deletes== named volumes and data
Leaving database files in the writable layer

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Volume vs bind mount?
How do you persist a database?
What happens to data when a container is removed?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Volumes for data that must live on, bind mounts for dev, tmpfs for secrets in RAM.

items: Each container gets its own ==network namespace==
A virtual interface (`veth`) pair joins it to a network
One end is `eth0` inside the container
The other end plugs into a bridge on the host
`bridge` (default): private subnet on the host, NAT out, containers reach each other by IP
User-defined bridge: ==built-in DNS==, so containers resolve each other by name
`host`: shares the host network stack, **no isolation**, no port mapping needed
`none`: no networking at all
`overlay`: multi-host networking for Swarm; `macvlan`: container gets its own MAC/LAN address
`-p 8080:80` maps host port 8080 to container port 80
Docker adds ==iptables DNAT== rules to do the mapping
Without `-p`, only containers on the same network can connect
`app` reaches Postgres at `db:5432`, resolved by DNS
Different user-defined networks **cannot** talk unless a container is attached to both
Using `localhost` to reach another container: it is the container itself, so use `db`
Publishing a database with `-p 5432:5432` when only an internal network is needed: it ==exposes it publicly==

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Bridge vs host vs overlay?
How do containers find each other by name?
What does `-p` actually do?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Use a user-defined bridge for name-based DNS and isolation, and publish only the ports the outside world needs.

items: ==Compose== defines multi-container apps in one `compose.yaml`
Top-level keys: `services`, `networks`, `volumes`
Also optional `configs` and `secrets` keys
A service takes `image` or `build`, plus `ports`, `environment`
Also `volumes`, `networks`, `depends_on`, `healthcheck`
Compose makes one ==default network== per project
Service names become **DNS** hostnames on it
`depends_on` sets start order only
With `condition: service_healthy` it waits for the healthcheck
`env_file`, `${VAR}` and a `.env` file feed variables
==Profiles== toggle optional services (debug, admin tools)
`compose.override.yaml` layers dev settings on top
Override is merged automatically with `compose.yaml`
Commands: `up -d`, `down`, `ps`, `logs -f`, `exec`, `build`, `config`
Assuming `depends_on` waits until the dependency is **ready**
Hardcoding secrets in `compose.yaml` and committing them
Use `.env` kept out of Git, or `secrets`, instead

blocks.title: Debug tip
blocks.text: Run `docker compose config` to see the merged, interpolated file.

items: What does `depends_on` guarantee?
How do Compose services discover each other?
When is Compose not enough?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Compose declares a whole stack in one file; service names are DNS, but only healthchecks mean ready.

items: `web` waits for `db` to pass `pg_isready`
`cache` has no `depends_on`, so it starts at once
`pgdata` survives `docker compose down` without `-v`

blocks.note: web reaches db at host db

items: A ==registry== stores and serves images over HTTP
A ==repository== holds the tagged versions of ONE image
`nginx:1.27` and `nginx:1.26` live in one repository
Reference: `registry/namespace/repo:tag`
{icon:docker} **Docker Hub** is the default registry
Push uploads only layers the registry ==lacks==
Pull fetches only layers the host is **missing**
Layers are shared by SHA256 digest, so reuse is free

blocks.text: Artifact Registry replaces GCR on Google Cloud. Public repos are open to pull; private ones need a login.

items: Tag a release with semver: `1.4.2`
Add the git SHA tag: `1.4.2-a1b2c3d`
Tags are mutable, so they can move
Pin deployments by ==digest==: `app@sha256:...`
A ==pull-through cache== proxies an upstream registry
It stores each layer after the first pull
Cuts Hub rate-limit pain and speeds up CI
Configure it as a daemon `registry-mirrors` entry
Deploying `:latest`: you can't tell or roll back the version
Pushing baked-in secrets to a public repo
Secrets stay in layers even after a later `rm`
Registry vs repository: what is the difference?
How do you version images?
How do you speed up pulls?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Tag with semver plus git SHA, deploy by digest, and never push secrets.

items: Containers are ==isolated processes==, not a hard security boundary
All containers share one host kernel, so a **kernel exploit** reaches the host
Container root is UID 0 on the host unless `userns` remaps it
Run as non-root: `USER app` in the Dockerfile
`--cap-drop ALL`, then `--cap-add` only what is needed
Avoid `--privileged`; add `--security-opt no-new-privileges`
`--read-only` filesystem, with `--tmpfs` for writable paths
==Seccomp== limits syscalls; ==AppArmor/SELinux== limit file access
Minimal bases (distroless, alpine) shrink attack surface and CVE count
Scan in CI with Trivy, Docker Scout or Grype
Pin versions or digests, and rebuild regularly for patches
Sign with cosign or Docker Content Trust, then verify before running
Build time: BuildKit `--mount=type=secret`
Runtime: Docker, Swarm or Kubernetes secrets
Never in `ENV` or image layers: both leak via `docker history`

blocks.note: Pin by digest, not a tag

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Are containers secure by default?
How do you handle secrets?
What does --privileged do?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: A shared kernel means least privilege, scanned and signed images, and real secrets.

blocks.title: Audit Tip
blocks.text: Run `docker scout cves <image>` before every release.

items: Mounting `/var/run/docker.sock`: that is **root on the host**
Running `--privileged` for convenience: all devices, no seccomp
Pulling unpinned images from unknown publishers
Putting passwords in `ENV` or `COPY`ed files
`docker inspect` shows config, mounts, networks, IPs, ==State.OOMKilled== and health
`docker exec -it <c> sh` explores a running container
Crash-looping? Use `--entrypoint sh` to override the entrypoint
`docker stats` live CPU, memory, I/O; `docker top` lists processes
`docker events` streams daemon events as they happen
`docker network inspect` shows subnet and attached containers
From inside, test DNS and ports with `curl`, `nslookup`, `nc`
Build: `docker build --progress=plain --no-cache .`
Isolate a failing stage with `--target <stage>`
Disk full: `docker system df`, then `docker system prune`
Add `--volumes` to prune only after **checking** what it removes
Fixing things by hand inside a container: edits **vanish** on recreate
Running `prune -a --volumes` on a host holding needed data
Bake fixes into the Dockerfile or compose file, then rebuild

blocks.title: Interview Point
blocks.text: A container keeps restarting: how do you diagnose it? What does exit code 137 mean? How do you debug a failing build?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Check ps -a and logs first, confirm with inspect, explore with exec, and fix the image, not the container.

items: `docker run` is one host, one container, no safety net
An ==orchestrator== adds scheduling, scaling and self-healing
Also rolling updates, service discovery and secrets
Healthchecks (`HEALTHCHECK` or Compose `healthcheck`) flag unhealthy containers for replacement
Set ==restart policies==, resource limits and log rotation
`json-file` with `max-size` / `max-file`, or a central driver
Stay **stateless**: state in volumes or external databases
Config in environment or secrets, not the image
Handle `SIGTERM` for graceful shutdown
Use `--init` (tini) to reap zombie processes

blocks.note: limits and rotation stop host starvation

items: Swarm: services, replicas, ==overlay== networks, rolling updates
Kubernetes: pods, deployments, services, ingress, autoscaling
Industry standard: more powerful and more complex
==Rolling update==: replace replicas a few at a time
==Blue/green==: switch traffic between two full stacks
==Canary==: send a small share of traffic to the new version
Tags immutable per release: never reuse `1.27`

a_bullets: Why use an orchestrator over plain `docker run`?
Swarm vs Kubernetes: when pick each?
How do you achieve zero-downtime deploys?

items: Stateful database in a container with no durable volume or backups
No resource limits: one noisy container starves the host
Reusing a mutable tag across releases
Healthcheck passes before traffic is routed
Old replicas get ==SIGTERM== and time to drain
Keep schema changes backward compatible

blocks.title: Grace Period
blocks.text: Set `stop_grace_period: 30s` so slow requests finish before SIGKILL.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Orchestrators keep stateless, healthchecked, limited containers running; roll out with immutable tags.

items: Q: Container vs image? An ==image== is the immutable template; a ==container== is a running instance
Q: Smaller image? Slim or distroless base, multi-stage, `.dockerignore`, merged and cleaned `RUN` layers
Q: Persist data? Named volumes or bind mounts, **never** the writable layer
Q: How do containers communicate? A ==user-defined network== with DNS by service name
Q: How to secure them? Run **non-root** and drop capabilities
Add a read-only filesystem and scanned, pinned images
Handle secrets properly: never bake them into layers
Treating containers like **pets**: patching them in place
Fix: change the Dockerfile, rebuild, and replace the container
Hand-patched containers drift and cannot be reproduced
One process concern per container, config via ==environment==
Pin base image versions or digests and rebuild regularly
Log to stdout/stderr; let the platform collect it
Keep images small, reproducible and tagged immutably

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Walk through containerizing an app, Dockerfile to deployment
Explain each choice: base image, stages, user, tag
How do you keep the result small, secure and reproducible?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Build small, pinned, non-root images, persist data outside the container, and rebuild instead of patching.

caption.text:
Everything you need before your Docker interview, in one handbook. 🐳

From "what even is a container?" to running Docker in production, this is the full fundamentals-to-production guide, written out as handwritten notes you can swipe through and revisit before the big day.

Topics covered:
✅ Docker at a Glance
✅ Docker Architecture and Runtime Internals
✅ Images and Layers
✅ Container Lifecycle and Runtime Control
✅ Dockerfile Essentials
✅ Build Optimization and Multi-Stage Builds
✅ Volumes and Storage
✅ Docker Networking
✅ Docker Compose
✅ Registries and Image Distribution
✅ Docker Security
✅ Debugging and Troubleshooting
✅ Production and Orchestration
✅ Interview Questions and Best Practices
✅ Docker Cheatsheet

Who it's for:
→ Developers and DevOps beginners learning Docker from scratch
→ Backend engineers who use Docker but want to understand what's under the hood
→ Anyone preparing for DevOps, backend or cloud interviews

Save this post so it's there when you need it, and share it with a teammate who's learning Docker.
